newsitem.title: USA: US Treasuries end lower in extremely low volume.
newsitem.headline: US Treasuries end lower in extremely low volume.

text.p: U.S. Treasuries ended lower on Monday, sliding in extremely light volume as traders set up short positions ahead of this week's two-year and five-year note auctions.

The bellwether 6.625 percent 30-year Treasury bond closed down 13/32 at 94-09/32 to yield 7.09 percent. The 6.25 percent two-year benchmark ended the session at 99-22/32, down 2/32 to yield 6.42 percent.

"Just the action of trying to get short for the auctions put pressure on the market," said Ted Ake, senior trader at Everen Securities Corp in Chicago. "You're seeing a ridiculously low amount of volume."
At 1600 EDT/2000 GMT, total GovPx volume remained shy of $50 billion -- well below normal levels.

Bonds ignored the only economic release on Monday's calendar -- A Treasury Department report which showed that the government posted a budget deficit of $21.32 billion in March, against a $47.07 billion deficit registered in March of last year.
Instead, traders focused on positioning ahead of the Treasury's auctions of $17.0 billion in two-year notes on Tuesday and $12.5 billion in five-year notes on Wednesday.
The market popped briefly higher in the morning, but began a slow, steady drift downward down after running into a technical ceiling.
"It's been a very quiet drift lower on almost no volume," said Patrick Dimick, treasury strategist and trader at UBS Securities.

"The 108-07/32 level was the high from last week and we drifted up close to there this morning and eventually faded from that resistance level," he added, referring to the lead June T-bond futures contract.
Dimick also said that a $400 million asset-backed bid list and a $400 million bid list in collateralized mortgage obligations could have been factors in the market's retreat.

Analysts said the market paid little attention to remarks from Federal Reserve Vice Chair Alice Rivlin, who said in a speech to the Employment Policy Foundation that the Fed was worried about a possible over-heating of the economy.
Rivlin also cited evidence of high consumer demand and the beginnings of wage increases, which she said would be passed along to consumer prices if the economy kept growing at its current pace.
Analysts said weakness in the dollar and a mid-session downturn in stocks also hurt Treasuries on Monday.

"On top of the uneasiness over the supply tomorrow and Wednesday, I think it was a combination of the continuing slide of the dollar and the nosedive that equities prices took at midday," Anthony Karydakis, senior financial economist at First Chicago Capital Markets, said of the market's decline.
The Dow ended down roughly 43 points at 6660, while the dollar pulled back to trade at 1.6960/70 marks at 1600 EDT/2000 GMT from 1.7030/40 at the open and 1.7115/20 on Friday.

"People are marking time until they get next week's critical economic reports out of the way," Karydakis said. "They want to see what these numbers hold in order to make a determination about the outcome of the next FOMC meeting and the overall near-term direction of rates."

Among next week's reports are the first quarter Employment Cost Index on Tuesday, an initial reading on first quarter GDP on Wednesday, the National Association of Purchasing Management's April manufacturing report on Thursday and April nonfarm payrolls data on Friday.
Three-month bills rates ended down two basis points at 5.13 percent, six-month bills rates settled unchanged at 5.40 percent and year-bill rates ended up three basis points at 5.62 percent.
The Treasury's bellwether five-year note ended down 5/32 at 99-15/32 to yield 6.75 percent and its ten-year note settled off 9/32 at 95-20/32 to yield 6.87 percent.
((-- N.A. Treasury Desk, 212-859-1673))
